blocks.prompt: The Giant With No Ground
blocks.text: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system. Every other planet could be packed inside it, and there would still be room left over. But Jupiter is not made of rock the way Earth is. It is a huge ball of gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, and it has no hard ground anywhere. A spaceship could not land on Jupiter. It would sink into thicker and thicker cloud until the weight of the air above it crushed the ship flat. The stripes you can see on Jupiter are bands of cloud. Some bands race one way. Some race the other. Where two bands rub past each other, storms are born. The biggest storm is called the Great Red Spot. It is wider than our whole planet, and people with telescopes have watched it spin for more than 150 years. Nobody knows exactly when it started. Jupiter has moons too. More than ninety of them. Four are big enough to spot with a small telescope. In 1610, an Italian scientist named Galileo pointed his telescope at Jupiter and saw those four moons circling it night after night. That changed everything. Most people back then believed every single thing in the sky went around Earth. Galileo could see with his own eyes that these four went around something else.

blocks.prompt: The Planet You Could Fall Through
blocks.text: Ask someone to name the biggest thing in the solar system and they will probably say the Sun. They are right. Ask for the second biggest, and the answer is Jupiter, and it is not a close contest. Jupiter contains more than twice as much material as every other planet added together. Roughly 1,300 Earths would fit inside it. Yet you could never stand on it. Jupiter is a gas giant. Its outer layers are hydrogen and helium, the same two elements that make up most of the Sun. There is no rock, no beach, no floor. If you fell into Jupiter, you would drop first through freezing clouds of ammonia, then through warmer layers, then into gas so tightly squeezed that it behaves more like a liquid than like air. The deeper you sank, the more the weight of everything above would press in on you. This is not a guess. In 1995, a small probe released by the Galileo spacecraft parachuted into those clouds on purpose. It sent measurements home for about an hour before the heat and the pressure destroyed it. It never reached anything solid, because there is nothing solid to reach. The stripes are clouds traveling in opposite directions at hundreds of miles per hour. Where opposing bands grind past one another, storms spin up. The Great Red Spot is the largest of them, a single storm wider than our entire planet, and astronomers have tracked it for more than 150 years. On Earth, a hurricane weakens and dies within a week or two, because it drags across land and cool water that starve it. Jupiter offers no land to drag across. So the storm just keeps turning.

blocks.prompt: The Storm That Will Not Die
blocks.text: Jupiter is built on a scale that resists imagination. Its diameter is about eleven times Earth's, and it outweighs every other planet in the solar system combined, twice over. It is also in a hurry. Despite its size, Jupiter completes one full rotation in under ten hours, which is the shortest day of any planet we know. Spin something that large that fast and it cannot hold a neat shape. Jupiter bulges at its equator and flattens at its poles, a squashed giant of a world. That rotation is what draws the stripes. Jupiter's atmosphere is stretched into bands that run parallel to the equator, alternating light zones and dark belts, each racing in the opposite direction to its neighbor. Along the seams where they scrape past each other, the atmosphere tears into swirls and storms. The most famous of these is the Great Red Spot, a rotating storm wide enough to swallow Earth, with winds near its edge running at hundreds of miles per hour. Astronomers have watched it continuously since the 1800s, and possibly far longer. Here is what makes it remarkable. A hurricane on Earth is a temporary thing. It draws its energy from warm ocean water, and the moment it crosses land or cool sea, it starves and unravels. It rarely lasts a fortnight. The Great Red Spot has no coastline to strike, no cold water to cross, and nothing beneath it but more atmosphere. It has been spinning for centuries. Even so, it is not permanent. Measurements taken over the last hundred years show the spot steadily shrinking. It was once wide enough to hold two or three Earths side by side. Today it holds barely one. Nobody can say with confidence whether it will fade out entirely or settle at a smaller size. Jupiter's other wonders are not on Jupiter at all. It is orbited by more than ninety moons. Ganymede, the largest, is bigger than the planet Mercury. Europa is wrapped in a shell of ice, and beneath that ice, evidence points to a salty ocean holding more water than every ocean on Earth put together. We call Jupiter the giant. Its moons may turn out to be the interesting part.

Would need roughly 80 times more mass to ignite

blocks.prompt: Almost a Star: The Planet That Missed
blocks.text: Jupiter is often called a failed star, and the phrase is doing a lot of work. It is not wrong about the ingredients. Jupiter is made of roughly the same stuff as the Sun, overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, gathered from the same disk of gas and dust that built everything else in the neighborhood. Had more material fallen into it, its core would have been squeezed harder and hotter, until hydrogen atoms began fusing into helium and the thing lit up. That is what a star is. But the shortfall was not narrow. Jupiter would need about eighty times its current mass to reach that threshold. Calling it a failed star is a bit like calling a pebble a failed mountain. It missed by a wide margin, and it became something far stranger instead. What happens inside Jupiter has no equivalent on Earth. Descend through the ammonia clouds and the pressure climbs relentlessly. There is no surface to cross, only gas that thickens until the distinction between gas and liquid stops meaning anything. Deeper still, the squeeze becomes so extreme that hydrogen abandons its normal behavior entirely. Its electrons are stripped loose and set free to roam, and the hydrogen begins to conduct electricity like a metal. This is liquid metallic hydrogen, an ocean of it, thousands of miles deep, churning as the planet whips around once every ten hours. That churning ocean is a dynamo, and it generates the most powerful magnetic field of any planet in the solar system. The field is enormous. It traps charged particles into radiation belts fierce enough to kill an unshielded astronaut, and it drives permanent auroras over Jupiter's poles that dwarf anything seen on Earth. The Juno spacecraft, in orbit since 2016, was built with a titanium vault around its electronics simply to survive taking the measurements. What Juno found underneath surprised people. Astronomers had expected a compact rocky core. Instead the gravity data suggests a fuzzy core, a smeared and partly dissolved center blending gradually into the layers above it, which hints that something violent happened early in Jupiter's history. There is a reason Jupiter keeps rearranging what we think we know. In January 1610, Galileo Galilei aimed a homemade telescope at the planet and noticed three small stars beside it. He watched for weeks. The stars moved, night after night, and never wandered away. There were four of them. They were not stars at all. They were worlds, circling Jupiter, plainly and repeatedly going around something that was not Earth. That single observation cracked the foundation of an entire cosmology, and the idea it supported would eventually put Galileo on trial. Four centuries later, those same moons are still the most interesting thing in the neighborhood. Ganymede outsizes the planet Mercury and generates a magnetic field of its own. Europa is sheathed in fractured ice, and beneath that shell the evidence points to a global saltwater ocean holding perhaps twice as much water as every ocean on Earth combined. The giant, in the end, may matter most for what it keeps close.
